entries.clue: Crazy long tale about saloon, perhaps, somewhere in Indian Ocean … (10)

indicatorNotes.about: 'about' turns the long tale round, so SAGA runs backwards

blocks.note: mad = crazy
a saga is a long tale; turned round it gives AGAS
a saloon is one kind of car, hence 'perhaps'

annotation.surface: Someone spins a wild yarn about a saloon bar, somewhere out in the Indian Ocean.
annotation.walkthrough: A saloon is the British word for a sedan car, not a bar. The ellipsis leads into 6 across, whose definition is also 'long tale'.
annotation.definitionFit: Madagascar is the large island in the Indian Ocean off the east coast of Africa.

entries.clue: Before start of evening, clean the floor that’s pine (4)

indicatorNotes.Before: the mopping comes before the E in the answer
indicatorNotes.start of: the start of 'evening' is its first letter, E

blocks.note: to mop is to clean the floor
first letter of evening

annotation.surface: Before evening someone cleans a pine floor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pine' looks like the wood of the floor, but it is the verb: to pine is to long for something gloomily.
annotation.definitionFit: To mope and to pine both mean to be listless and miserable.

entries.clue: Soupçon of fly (4)

blocks.note: French for a hint or tiny amount, as of a seasoning
the verb: to hurry off at speed

annotation.surface: A tiny amount of fly, like a cook's pinch of something.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fly' looks like the insect, but it is the verb to hurry off.
annotation.definitionFit: Both are plain synonyms: a splash of milk in tea is a small measure, and rushing off to catch a train is flying.

entries.clue: Attacks poor and gambles the lot (4,3,5)

blocks.note: goes for = attacks
broke = poor, penniless

annotation.surface: A desperate person turns on the poor and bets everything.
annotation.walkthrough: The phrase splits neatly: the first two words are the attack, the last is the poverty.
annotation.definitionFit: To go for broke is to risk everything on one attempt.

entries.clue: Presents – or hides from view? (7)

blocks.note: shows, as a cinema or TV channel shows a film
a screen hides what is behind it

annotation.surface: A puzzle about whether showing something and hiding it can be the same act.
annotation.walkthrough: The two senses are opposites, which is the point of the question mark.
annotation.definitionFit: Screens means both shows on a screen and shields from sight.

entries.clue: Believes in counterfeits (7)

blocks.note: to assume is to take as true
to assume an air or a name is to put it on falsely

annotation.surface: Someone has faith in forged goods.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Believes in' reads as one phrase, but 'in' only joins; 'counterfeits' is a verb, as in feigns.
annotation.definitionFit: He assumes she is right; he assumes a false accent.

entries.clue: … eastern image in long tale (4)

blocks.note: E = eastern, as on a compass
pic = picture, an image

annotation.surface: Continuing from 1 across, an eastern picture appears within a long story.
annotation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries on from 1 across, where 'long tale' gave SAGA; here the same phrase is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: An epic is a long narrative poem or story of heroic deeds.

entries.clue: President concealing ‘legal’ cash for those seeking power (10)

blocks.note: Pres. is the abbreviation for President
legal tender is money that must be accepted in payment

annotation.surface: A president hides dubiously 'legal' money meant for power-seekers.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks pair 'legal' with cash to make legal tender, of which only TENDER is used.
annotation.definitionFit: A pretender is a claimant to a throne or title.

entries.clue: In conversation, parish representative’s advisor (10)

indicatorNotes.In conversation: spoken, the word matches another spelling

blocks.note: a parish councillor sits on the parish council

annotation.surface: Talk turns to the local council member's adviser.
annotation.walkthrough: A parish council is the lowest tier of English local government; its members are councillors, which sounds identical to the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word covers anyone whose job is to give advice, from a therapist to a legal adviser.

entries.clue: Sterilise (milk perhaps) that’s in and out of sight, they say (10)

indicatorNotes.they say: what people say out loud, not how it is written

blocks.note: something that has gone in and out of sight has gone past your eyes

annotation.surface: A milk that flickers in and out of view, it is said.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay is a phrase to be paraphrased first: whatever passes in and out of sight goes past your eyes.
annotation.definitionFit: Pasteurising milk heats it to kill bacteria, a form of sterilising.

entries.clue: File’s one showing fellows by university (4)

annotation.definitionNote: on a computer, File is one menu, so 'File's one' means a menu

indicatorNotes.by: 'by' in its sense of beside: the university letter stands right beside the fellows, placed after them

blocks.note: fellows = men
U = university

annotation.surface: A college file lists its fellows by university.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fellows' and 'university' suggest academic records, but 'File' is the menu at the top left of a computer program.
annotation.definitionFit: File is one of the menus in a program's menu bar.

entries.clue: Robert skates erratically: it’s a way of crossing the water (12)

annotation.definition: a way of crossing the water

indicatorNotes.erratically: the letters move erratically into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

annotation.surface: Robert wobbles across the ice on skates to get over a frozen lake.
annotation.walkthrough: Skating suggests crossing water that is frozen; the answer crosses it by swimming.
annotation.definitionFit: Breaststroke is a swimming stroke, one way to cross water.

entries.clue: Freak’s metal bananas in second-hand stalls (4,7)

indicatorNotes.bananas: bananas = crazy, so the letters go wild

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters, including the S of 's

annotation.surface: An oddball's scrap metal and bananas turn up at junk stalls.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe S of 'Freak's' is part of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A description rather than a synonym: these open-air markets are made up of stalls selling used goods, once supposedly with fleas in them.

entries.clue: Fools’ son intended to lose heart in test (10)

indicatorNotes.to lose heart: MEANT loses its middle letter, A

S = son
MEANT (intended) without its central A

annotation.surface: A foolish family's son was supposed to lose courage during an exam.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lose heart' reads as losing courage; here it means dropping the middle letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, in the school sense: an exam or piece of coursework that measures what a pupil knows.

entries.clue: Echoing intemperate petitioner (10)

annotation.definitionNote: 'echoing' is read as a noun, the act of echoing

indicatorNotes.intemperate: unrestrained, so the letters run wild

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

annotation.surface: An angry petitioner keeps shouting the same thing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Echoing' looks like an adjective describing the petitioner; it is the definition, a noun meaning saying again.
annotation.definitionFit: Read as a verbal noun, as in 'the echoing of her words', it means saying or sounding the same thing again.

entries.clue: Primarily Spanish in etymology: ranges, rising apexes serrated? (7)

annotation.definition: Primarily Spanish in etymology: ranges, rising apexes serrated?

indicatorNotes.Primarily: take the first letter of each word that follows

blocks.note: first letters of the seven words

annotation.surface: A dictionary note: these mountain ranges have a Spanish name and saw-toothed peaks.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: sierra is Spanish for saw, from the jagged skyline of the peaks.
annotation.definitionFit: Sierras are mountain ranges with jagged peaks; the word is Spanish, from Latin serra, a saw.

entries.clue: Cold – wearing summer footwear – disgrace! (7)

indicatorNotes.wearing: C is wearing SANDAL, so sits inside it

blocks.note: a sandal is summer footwear
C = cold, as on a tap

annotation.surface: Someone scolds a person for wearing sandals in the cold.
annotation.walkthrough: C goes in after the first letter: S(C)ANDAL.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym used as an exclamation: 'It's a disgrace!' and 'It's a scandal!' are the same outraged cry.

entries.clue: Dope and rye – wasted – this’ll help you see straight (3-4)

indicatorNotes.wasted: wasted = drunk or ruined, so the letters reel

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters; 'and' just joins them

annotation.walkthrough: 'See straight' suggests sobering up after the drugs and drink; the answer literally helps the eyes.
annotation.definitionFit: An eye-drop is medicine put in the eye to help vision.

entries.clue: Criticise a revolutionary style (7)

taken as written

annotation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary style' reads as one phrase, but the definition is just 'style'.

entries.clue: Some confront a rioter in Canadian province (7)

entries.clue: Incredibly wide, rustling up cocaine (7)

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

entries.clue: Bug … bear … cricket, perhaps (5,6)

blocks.note: to stick something is to bear it, as in can't stick him
a cricket is one insect, hence 'perhaps'

annotation.surface: A list of creatures: a bug, a bear, a cricket.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bear' is the verb to tolerate, not the animal. 'Stick' for tolerate is informal British.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose, everyday sense: 'bug' is casual for any small creepy-crawly, and this twig-like creature qualifies.

entries.clue: Old Testament figure seen in chocolate sauce (4)

entries.clue: Flipping prison sentence to throw out (4)
